podcast.title: "Christian Underground"
podcast.body: The self-sustaining ecosystem of Christian bands performing in Christian-owned clubs, signing with Christian record labels, and selling CDs through Christian bookstores was often referred to as the "Christian Underground." "Some called it the Christian Underground."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Built-in Audience
podcast.body: The genre benefits from a substantial pre-existing audience, estimated to include over 180 million Americans who are potential consumers. "Christians have a built-in audience of over 180 million Americans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Commentary on Disaster Movies
podcast.body: The Domains, a popular Christian rock group of the 1970s, offered a syndicated music column in Catholic publications. In an October 10, 1975, column for the *Lake Shore Visitor* from Erie, Pennsylvania, a representative of the group suggested that disaster movies like *Jaws* served as an escape for a nation "tired of serious subjects" like presidential judgment, war, economic woes, and oil company complexities, providing a "healing toy" during a period of weariness. "The domains were a popular christian rock group of the 70s and someone from the group wrote a syndicated music column for a variety of Catholic publications."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 44 - Streaking, Werewolves, Sharks, & Drinking - 70s Novelty Songs

podcast.title: Development of the Christian Underground
podcast.body: By the late 1990s, a sophisticated infrastructure emerged to support Christian rock, including Christian-owned clubs, record labels, and bookstores. This ecosystem was sometimes referred to as the "Christian Underground." "Christian bands played in Christian-owned clubs and signed a Christian-owned record label so sold their CDs through Christian bookstores."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Condemnation (1950s)
podcast.body: In the 1950s, upon the advent of rock and roll, religious leaders of all denominations universally denounced it as "the music of the devil," deeming it immoral and evil. Some churches even conducted public record burnings, with artists like Elvis and The Beatles being primary targets. "When rock and roll first came on the scene in the 1950s, leaders of all denominations and creeds declared it to be the music of the devil. Rock and roll was condemned from pulpits everywhere as immoral and evil."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Stereotypes
podcast.body: Throughout the 1980s, Christian rock was often stereotyped as "well scrub preaching from behind a guitar," with mainstream fans perceiving the music as weak and watered down, clashing with rock and roll's rebellious spirit. "Mainstream fans found the music weak in water down and wasn't rock and roll supposed to be about rebellion?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence as a Distinct Genre (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: By the end of the 1970s, Christian rock, along with Christian pop, had established itself as a distinct musical genre. Kerry Livgren of Kansas, for example, became a Christian rock artist after his born-again conversion in late 1979. "By the time we get to the end of the 1970s, Christian rock and pop were their own genres."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Evolving Stereotypes (Late 1990s)
podcast.body: Towards the end of the 1990s, the negative stereotypes associated with Christian rock began to diminish. Bands increasingly attracted fans based on their sound and musical quality, rather than solely their message. Their music became positive and current, less preachy, and visually and sonically resembled mainstream bands, albeit with a noticeable absence of typical rock and roll themes like sex and drugs. "By the end of the decade the various stereotypes began to fall by the wayside. Instead of weak and safe imitations of the real thing these bands began to attract fans for their sound and not their message."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fear of Mainstream Perception
podcast.body: Conversely, Christian rock bands also expressed concern about being perceived as "too wholesome" by the secular world, fearing they would be dismissed as "sermonizers and proselytizers" and thus "shot down based on preconceived notions." "At the same time, these bands are worried about being too wholesome for the rest of the world. That they'll be perceived as sermonizers and proselytizers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Growing Music Segment
podcast.body: Christian Rock is highlighted as one of the rare segments within the music industry that is actively growing and increasing in profitability. "It's one of the few segments of the music industry that's actually growing and becoming more profitable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Growing and Profitable Segment
podcast.body: Christian Rock is highlighted as one of the few segments within the music industry that is actively experiencing growth and increasing profitability. "It's one of the few segments of the music industry that's actually growing and becoming more profitable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Historical Oxymoron
podcast.body: For decades, the concept of "Christian rock" was considered oxymoronic, as "good Christians" were not believed to "rock," and electric guitars were deemed inappropriate for hymns. "There was no such thing as Christian rock for decades."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: INXS's Brief Venture
podcast.body: The band INXS, early in its career, briefly attempted to enter the Christian rock market. This endeavor, however, was very short-lived, lasting only "about a minute." "and originally the idea was to try to break into the Christian rock market, which lasted about a minute."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Infrastructure Development (1990s)
podcast.body: By the late 1990s, the Christian rock scene had significantly broadened, with an increase in new groups, louder guitars, and heavier beats, including the emergence of Christian speed and thrash scenes in California. A sophisticated infrastructure was built to support this music, including Christian-owned clubs, record labels, and bookstores. "By the late 1990s Christian rock had really opened up. More groups were formed. The guitar got louder and the beads got heavier."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Internal Schisms and Judgmentalism
podcast.body: The Christian underground experienced "a series of schisms." Bands crossing into the mainstream worried about alienating their Christian fanbase by appearing too negative or straying into territory that could be interpreted as immoral, offensive, or anti-God. Some factions of Christian fans were highly judgmental, evaluating bands based on "Gods Per Minute" (GPMs)—the number of times "God" was invoked in lyrics—to determine a band's "holiness." "There were a series of schisms within the Christian underground. Some of the bands we've heard on this program are worried about alienating the Christian fans as they cross over into the mainstream."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mainstream Industry Misunderstanding
podcast.body: The mainstream music industry often struggles to comprehend and manage Christian bands and their values, being more accustomed to promoting themes of rebellion, sex, and violence. "Most of the mainstream music industry doesn't know what to do with these bands and their values. It's made billions by pushing songs about rebellion and sex and violence and infidelity and immorality and even criminal behavior."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mainstream Perceptions vs. Crossover Ambitions
podcast.body: Christian rock bands often face a dilemma: they fear being "too wholesome" for the mainstream, which could lead to them being dismissed as "sermonizers and proselytizers" based on preconceived notions. "At the same time, these bands are worried about being too wholesome for the rest of the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mid-90s Market Growth
podcast.body: The market for Christian rock experienced rapid growth in the mid-1990s, with youth groups and churches hosting concerts. These events were considered safe for parents and helped spread awareness of the bands. "The market for Christian rock grew quickly in the middle 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ongoing Condemnation
podcast.body: Even with the genre's evolution, the belief that rock music itself is evil persists, with some people actively condemning Christian rock bands for "perverting Christianity" by playing such music. "Some people believe that these bands, no matter what their veneer, are perverting Christianity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Oxymoronic Concept Historically
podcast.body: For decades, the very idea of "Christian rock" was considered contradictory, or "oxymoronic," because "Good Christians simply did not rock," and electric guitars were not seen as appropriate for hymns. "There was no such thing as Christian rock for decades. The concept was oxymoronic. Good Christians simply did not rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Parallel Universe Existence
podcast.body: For an extended period, Christian rock existed within its "own parallel universe," largely separate from the mainstream music scene, though an increasing number of bands are now crossing over. "Until now, Christian rock has existed in its own paradol universe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Persistent "Evil Rock" Belief
podcast.body: Despite the evolution and growth of Christian rock, the belief that "rock music is evil" remains prevalent among some individuals. These critics argue that Christian bands, regardless of their presentation, are "perverting Christianity," often quoting scripture to support their condemnation of groups like Creed, Jars of Clay, and MXPX. "The concept that rock music is evil is still alive and well. Some people believe that these bands, no matter what their veneer, are perverting Christianity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Schisms and Fan Judgment
podcast.body: The Christian underground experienced internal divisions. Bands crossing over to the mainstream worried about alienating Christian fans if their content was perceived as negative, immoral, offensive, or "anti-god." Some Christian fans are described as very judgmental, particularly concerning the "GPMs" (Gods Per Minute) in lyrics. "Some factions of Christian rock fans can be very judgmental without the requisite number of GPMs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shifting Perception in the Late 90s
podcast.body: Towards the end of the 1990s, stereotypes associated with Christian rock began to diminish. Bands started attracting fans based on their sound rather than solely their message, offering positive, current, and less preachy music that resembled mainstream rock while notably lacking themes of sex and drugs. "Instead of weak and safe imitations of the real thing, these bands began to attract fans for their sound and not their message."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Subtle Religious Message
podcast.body: Many Christian Rock bands produce music that sounds mainstream, with listeners often unaware of the religious orientation of the artists unless explicitly told. "And here's the weird thing, unless you even know, you'd never guess that these bands were all about God."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Toughening and Growth (1980s)
podcast.body: Throughout the 1980s, Christian rock experienced growth and became "toughen up," despite a prevailing stereotype that it was "weak and watered down" and involved "well scrub preaching from behind a guitar" in the eyes of mainstream fans. "Christian rock continued to grow and toughen up throughout the 1980s but for most people Christian rock was still stereotyped as well scrub preaching from behind a guitar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Youth Group and Church Support
podcast.body: In the mid-1990s, the Christian rock market expanded rapidly, partly due to youth groups and churches organizing shows. These events were considered "the safest type of concert any parent could hope to find," helping to spread word-of-mouth for many bands. "The market for Christian rock grew quickly in the middle of the 90s. Youth groups and churches began to put on shows which is about the safest type of concert any parent could hope to find."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
